newsitem.title: UK: PRESS DIGEST - British business press - April 16.
newsitem.headline: PRESS DIGEST - British business press - April 16.

text.p: Prepared for Reuters by The Broadcast Monitoring Company
DAILY TELEGRAPH
-- CO-OP CHIEF CALLS FOR CWS MERGER

David Robey, the new head of Co-operative Retail Society's food arm, formerly of Safeway and Tesco, has spoken in favour of CRS and the Co-operative Wholesale Society merging. Combined, the two would have combined sales of 4.7 billion stg. CWS faces takeover pressure from Andrew Regan of Lancia Trust. Robey faces opposition to his view from the chief executives of both CRS and CWS.
-- ABF FIRES NATWEST AS YEN FAILS TO PERFORM

Associated British Foods yesterday fired NatWest Group as adviser to its investment fund, a post it has held for 11 years. The bank had invested heavily in yen- dominated instruments, which were hit by the yen's severe depreciation.
-- BRISTOL & WEST CHIEF EYES SOCIETY TAKEOVER

Bristol & West chief John Burke yesterday said he wants to take over another society, and that he is eyeing one in particular. He spoke after B&W members approved its takeover by the Bank of Ireland. B&W and Northern Rock yesterday both approved their societies' conversions, now subject to Building Societies Commission approval.
THE TIMES
-- EURO DOUBTS PUSH POUND TO FIVE-YEAR HIGH

The pound rose to its highest level for almost five years yesterday after Alexandre Lamfalussy, president of the European Monetary Institute, voiced doubts that the single currency would proceed on schedule. He also confirmed the institute would not insist on euro candidates meeting all the criteria laid down in the Maastricht Treaty.
-- BT INVESTORS BACK 13 BILLION POUND MCI DEAL

British Telecom yesterday won shareholder approval for the 13 billion stg takeover of MCI, the American long-distance telephone company. About 98.5 percent of shareholders voted in favour of the deal, which creates a company to be called Concert, the world's fourth largest telecoms group.
-- QUANT TO JOIN HOUSE OF FRASER BOARD

Mary Quant is to become a non-executive director of the House of Fraser department stores group. The troubled retail group has been criticized as being behind the times, and in January it announced plans to cut 1,000 jobs and clear stock. Shares were up 0.5p to 164p yesterday and 1996 results are due tomorrow.
THE GUARDIAN
-- LEADING DEALERS FEAR SHARES MAY FALL SOON AFTER BLAIR VICTORY

The Reuters Larger Companies survey revealed that a Labour victory is yet to be priced into the stock market. Nearly half of fund managers expect shares to peak in the next three months -- a result analysts regard as an indictment on Labour, considering the party's huge polls lead.
-- NATWEST STAFF HIT OUT AT 'DIRTY TACTICS'

NatWest has been accused of 'dirty tactics' in attempting to prevent NatWest Staff Association general secretary Rory Murphy from being elected to the board. The company has sent a letter to staff reminding them Murphy can only be elected to replace existing directors, all of whom are backed by the board. Murphy is standing to attempt to shield the bank's profit-related pay scheme from the impact of the 90 million stg derivatives loss at NatWest Markets.
-- CLEAN UP ON DIRTY CASH, CITY TOLD

John Moscow, assistant district attorney for Manhattan, warned yesterday that black money deals were being routed through the City of London from New York. He will speak to British bankers at a symposium later this month on the blind-eye strategy many British institutions apply to criminal business. He warns the USA is adopting tough tactics to deal with dollar money-laundering outside the United States.
THE INDEPENDENT
-- CLARK FAMILY IN SELL-OFF BONANZA

Around 400 family shareholders in the Clarks shoe business are to receive a large payout after the company sold its factory outlet retail business for 80 million stg yesterday. The outlets will be sold to property group MEPC and 53 million stg of the money raised distributed to shareholders.
-- CALENERGY ALLOWS FOR WINDFALL TAX

The U.S.'s CalEnergy, which took over Northern Electric last December, have made provision against the windfall tax threatened by Labour. The 1996 report, released yesterday, shows a liability against the levy has been established. Analysts suggest it will be about 90 million to 100 million stg.
-- LACK OF RAIN THREATENS THE NATION'S CUPPA

Tea prices are soaring, due to the combination of drought in Kenya, rain shortage in Sri Lanka, and late harvest in India. Since 1995, the price of a kilogram of tea has doubled to almost 1.22 stg. However, the Tea Council played down the threat.
